hook.text: Computers only understand two symbols: 0 and 1. Everything else is built from those.

buildup.text: Binary uses base 2. Each digit doubles in value: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, and so on.

discovery.text: The number 13 in binary is 1101 — that's 8 + 4 + 0 + 1.

twist.text: Transistors make binary natural — on is 1, off is 0. No need for ten states.

climax.text: Every photo, song, message, and video on your phone is just a stream of 0s and 1s.

punchline.text: Two symbols, infinite possibilities — binary runs the digital world.

quiz.question: What is the decimal value of the binary number 1101?

hook.text: A single binary digit is a bit. Eight bits together form a byte.

buildup.text: One byte can represent 256 different values — from 00000000 to 11111111.

discovery.text: A kilobyte is 1,024 bytes. A megabyte is about a million. A terabyte is a trillion.

twist.text: A single character of text takes one byte. A smartphone photo takes several million.

climax.text: The entire internet generates about 400 million terabytes of data every single day.

punchline.text: Eight tiny switches — one byte — can hold a letter, a color, or a sound sample.

quiz.question: How many different values can one byte represent?

hook.text: Writing long binary strings is tedious. Hexadecimal packs four bits into one symbol.

buildup.text: Hex uses 0-9 and A-F. The hex digit 'F' represents binary 1111, which is decimal 15.

discovery.text: The binary number 11111111 becomes FF in hex. Much easier to read and type.

twist.text: Web colors use hex: #FF0000 is red, #00FF00 is green, #0000FF is blue.

climax.text: Memory addresses, MAC addresses, and error codes are all written in hex for readability.

punchline.text: Hex turns eight messy bits into two clean characters — readability wins.

quiz.question: What binary value does the hex digit 'A' represent?

topics.title: Two's Complement: Negative Numbers in Binary

hook.text: Binary has no minus sign. So how does a computer represent negative numbers?

buildup.text: Two's complement flips all bits and adds 1. The result represents the negative value.

discovery.text: In 8-bit two's complement, 11111111 is -1, not 255. The top bit signals the sign.

twist.text: Addition works the same for positive and negative — the hardware doesn't need a subtractor.

climax.text: Every processor uses two's complement for signed integers — it simplifies circuits enormously.

punchline.text: Flip the bits, add one — suddenly binary can go below zero.

quiz.question: Why is two's complement preferred for signed numbers?
options: It allows the same addition circuit to handle both positive and negative numbers
It doubles the range of representable numbers
It eliminates the need for binary altogether

hook.text: Integers are easy in binary. But how do computers handle 3.14 or 0.001?

buildup.text: Floating point splits a number into sign, exponent, and mantissa — like scientific notation.

discovery.text: IEEE 754 defines 32-bit and 64-bit formats. Every computer follows the same standard.

twist.text: 0.1 + 0.2 ≠ 0.3 in floating point — tiny rounding errors are inevitable.

climax.text: Graphics, physics simulations, and AI training all depend on fast floating-point hardware.

punchline.text: Computers approximate decimals — close for rockets, tricky for banks.

quiz.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal exactly 0.3 in floating point?
options: Computers can't add numbers smaller than 1
Some decimal fractions can't be represented exactly in binary, causing tiny rounding errors
The IEEE 754 standard intentionally rounds all results down

hook.text: George Boole invented an algebra where variables are only true or false. 1 or 0.

buildup.text: AND, OR, and NOT replace multiplication, addition, and negation in this algebra.

discovery.text: De Morgan's laws let you swap ANDs and ORs by flipping the NOTs. Simplification follows.

twist.text: Boole wrote his laws in 1854 — nearly a century before digital computers existed.

climax.text: Shannon's 1937 thesis showed Boolean algebra maps directly onto electrical switching circuits.

punchline.text: An algebra with only two values — Boole gave computers their native language.

quiz.question: Who showed that Boolean algebra maps to electrical circuits?
options: George Boole in 1854
Claude Shannon in his 1937 thesis
Alan Turing in 1950

topics.title: AND, OR, NOT: The Three Foundations

hook.text: Three simple operations — AND, OR, NOT — are enough to build any digital circuit.

buildup.text: AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1. OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1.

discovery.text: NOT flips the input: 0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0. Just two transistors in CMOS.

twist.text: Any Boolean function — no matter how complex — can be built from just these three gates.

climax.text: A modern processor is billions of AND, OR, and NOT gates wired together.

punchline.text: Three tiny rules, billions of gates — that's all a computer needs to think.

quiz.question: When does an AND gate output 1?
options: When at least one input is 1
When both inputs are 1
When both inputs are 0

hook.text: A NAND gate is an AND followed by a NOT. It's simple — and it can do everything.

buildup.text: NAND outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1. Any other combination gives 1.

discovery.text: You can build AND, OR, NOT, and any logic function using only NAND gates.

twist.text: NOR gates are also universal. Early Apollo guidance computers were built entirely from NOR gates.

climax.text: Chip designers often use NAND-only or NOR-only libraries to simplify manufacturing.

punchline.text: One gate type to rule them all — NAND is the universal building block.

quiz.question: What makes NAND a 'universal' gate?
options: It is the fastest gate to manufacture
Any logic function can be built using only NAND gates
It uses the least power of any gate type

hook.text: XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ. Same inputs give 0. It detects disagreement.

discovery.text: XOR is perfect for binary addition: 1 + 1 = 10 — the XOR gives the sum bit, AND gives the carry.

twist.text: XOR with the same value twice returns the original — the basis of simple encryption.

climax.text: Adders, checksums, parity checks, and encryption all rely on XOR operations.

punchline.text: Are the inputs different? XOR says yes or no — the simplest comparator.

quiz.question: What does XOR output when both inputs are the same?
options: It depends on whether the inputs are both 0 or both 1

hook.text: A truth table lists every possible input combination and its output. No ambiguity.

buildup.text: Two inputs give four rows. Three inputs give eight. N inputs give 2^N rows.

discovery.text: From a truth table, you can derive the exact Boolean expression for any logic function.

twist.text: Karnaugh maps group adjacent rows to simplify expressions — fewer gates, cheaper circuits.

climax.text: Every digital circuit begins as a truth table before it becomes transistors on silicon.

punchline.text: List every input. Write every output. The truth table hides nothing.

quiz.question: How many rows does a truth table for a 4-input function have?

topics.title: Logic Levels: What Counts as 0 or 1

hook.text: A digital 1 isn't exactly 5 volts. It's anything above a threshold. Below is 0.

buildup.text: TTL logic treats 0-0.8 V as low and 2.0-5.0 V as high. The gap is a noise margin.

discovery.text: Modern CMOS uses 1.8 V, 1.2 V, or even 0.8 V supplies — lower voltage, lower power.

twist.text: If a signal lands in the undefined zone between high and low, the gate output is unpredictable.

climax.text: Level shifters translate between different voltage families so chips can talk to each other.

punchline.text: Digital isn't perfect 0 or 5 — it's close enough, with a safety margin.

quiz.question: What is a 'noise margin' in digital logic?
options: The maximum audible noise a circuit can produce
The voltage gap between guaranteed logic levels that protects against interference
The power consumed by a gate when switching

hook.text: Logic gates don't respond instantly. Each gate adds a tiny delay to the signal.

buildup.text: Propagation delay is the time from input change to output change — typically picoseconds.

discovery.text: The longest path through a circuit — the critical path — sets the maximum clock speed.

twist.text: Adding more gates for complex logic also adds delay. Speed and complexity trade off.

climax.text: Chip designers optimize critical paths obsessively to squeeze out every last gigahertz.

punchline.text: Every gate costs time. The critical path sets the speed limit.

quiz.question: What determines a circuit's maximum clock speed?
options: The total number of gates in the circuit
The propagation delay along the longest (critical) path
The supply voltage of the logic family

hook.text: Computers add numbers using gates, not memorized tables. Hardware does the math.

buildup.text: A half adder uses XOR for the sum bit and AND for the carry bit. Two gates, one-bit addition.

discovery.text: A full adder adds three bits — two inputs plus a carry-in — producing sum and carry-out.

twist.text: Chain 64 full adders and you get a 64-bit adder — but the carry ripples through slowly.

climax.text: Carry-lookahead adders predict carries in parallel — trading gates for speed.

punchline.text: XOR for the sum, AND for the carry — addition built from logic gates.

quiz.question: What does a half adder lack that a full adder has?
options: A sum output
A carry-in input from a previous stage
An XOR gate

hook.text: A multiplexer picks one of many inputs and sends it to the output. A digital switch.

buildup.text: Select lines choose which input to pass through. Two select lines handle four inputs.

discovery.text: Any Boolean function can be implemented with a large enough multiplexer — it's universal.

twist.text: Demultiplexers do the reverse — route one input to one of many outputs.

climax.text: Network routers, memory buses, and display controllers all use multiplexing.

punchline.text: Many inputs, one output — the multiplexer picks the winner.

quiz.question: How many select lines does a 4-to-1 multiplexer need?

hook.text: A decoder takes a binary number and activates exactly one output line. Binary in, one-hot out.

buildup.text: A 3-to-8 decoder turns a 3-bit input into one of eight output lines going high.

discovery.text: Memory chips use decoders to select the right row and column for each address.

twist.text: Encoders do the reverse — they convert one active line back into its binary code.

climax.text: Instruction decoders in CPUs break opcodes into control signals that drive execution.

punchline.text: Feed in a number, light up one line — the decoder translates binary addresses.

quiz.question: How many outputs does a 4-to-16 decoder have?

topics.title: ALU: The Calculator Inside the Processor

hook.text: The ALU — Arithmetic Logic Unit — does the math and logic inside every CPU.

buildup.text: It combines adders, shifters, and logic gates. Control signals select the operation.

discovery.text: One ALU can add, subtract, AND, OR, XOR, shift, and compare — all with the same hardware.

twist.text: Modern CPUs have multiple ALUs working in parallel — executing several operations per clock cycle.

climax.text: GPUs contain thousands of simple ALUs — perfect for parallel math in graphics and AI.

punchline.text: Add, compare, shift — the ALU does math one operation at a time.

quiz.question: What distinguishes a GPU from a CPU in terms of ALUs?
options: GPUs have one very fast ALU; CPUs have many slow ones
GPUs contain thousands of simple ALUs for massive parallelism
GPUs don't use ALUs — they use dedicated graphics hardware

hook.text: How does a computer decide if A > B? A comparator circuit answers in one clock cycle.

buildup.text: It subtracts B from A and checks the sign bit. Negative means A < B. Zero means equal.

discovery.text: Three output flags: greater-than, less-than, and equal — exactly one is active.

twist.text: Cascading comparators handle wider numbers — each stage feeds its result to the next.

climax.text: Sorting algorithms, conditional branches, and priority encoders all depend on comparators.

punchline.text: Is A bigger? Subtract and check the sign — comparison made hardware-simple.

quiz.question: How does a hardware comparator determine if A < B?
options: It counts the number of 1-bits in each number
It subtracts B from A and checks if the result is negative
It compares each bit from left to right using XOR gates

hook.text: Shifting a binary number left by one is the same as multiplying by 2. No adder needed.

buildup.text: A simple shifter moves bits one position per clock. Too slow for big shifts.

discovery.text: A barrel shifter uses layers of multiplexers to shift by any amount in one clock cycle.

twist.text: Rotate operations wrap bits around — nothing is lost, just repositioned.

climax.text: Cryptography, compression, and floating-point normalization all require fast shifting.

punchline.text: Shift left to multiply, shift right to divide — moving bits is instant math.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of a barrel shifter over a simple shifter?
options: It uses fewer transistors
It can shift by any number of positions in one clock cycle
It doesn't require a clock signal

hook.text: Logic gates forget — change the input and the output changes instantly. Memory needs something more.

buildup.text: Cross-connect two NOR gates and the output stays put even when the input changes. Memory.

discovery.text: This SR latch has Set and Reset inputs. Set makes it store 1. Reset makes it store 0.

twist.text: Setting both S and R to 1 is forbidden — the output becomes unpredictable.

climax.text: Latches are the simplest memory elements — the foundation of registers and RAM.

punchline.text: Two gates feeding back into each other — the tiniest memory in digital logic.

quiz.question: What makes an SR latch different from a simple gate?
options: It can add two numbers together
Its feedback loop lets it hold a value even after the input changes
It uses three or more inputs instead of two

hook.text: A latch is transparent — it passes data whenever enabled. Flip-flops only capture on a clock edge.

buildup.text: The D flip-flop captures the input at the rising edge of the clock and holds it until the next edge.

discovery.text: Edge triggering prevents data from racing through — each stage gets one clean snapshot.

twist.text: Setup and hold times define a window around the clock edge — data must be stable during it.

climax.text: Every register in every processor is built from D flip-flops synchronized to the clock.

punchline.text: One clock edge, one snapshot — flip-flops keep circuits in step.

quiz.question: What triggers a D flip-flop to capture its input?
options: Any change in the data input
The rising (or falling) edge of the clock signal
A high level on the enable pin

hook.text: Line up 64 flip-flops and you get a 64-bit register — one word of CPU storage.

buildup.text: All flip-flops share the same clock. On each edge, the entire word updates at once.

discovery.text: CPUs have dozens of registers: program counter, instruction register, general-purpose registers.

twist.text: Registers are the fastest memory — accessed in a single clock cycle, unlike cache or RAM.

climax.text: ARM's architecture has 31 general-purpose 64-bit registers — the core of its data path.

punchline.text: Flip-flops in a row — the fastest memory a processor has.

quiz.question: Why are registers faster than cache or RAM?
options: They use larger transistors that switch more quickly
They are built from flip-flops directly inside the CPU, accessed in one clock cycle
They store data in analog form, avoiding digital conversion delays

hook.text: A counter increments its stored value by one on every clock pulse. Pure counting in hardware.

buildup.text: A 4-bit binary counter cycles from 0000 to 1111 and wraps around — 16 states.

discovery.text: Ripple counters chain flip-flops — each one toggles the next. Simple but the carry ripples.

twist.text: Synchronous counters update all bits at once. Faster but use more gates.

climax.text: Timers, frequency dividers, and address generators all use counters.

punchline.text: Tick, tick, tick — a counter turns clock pulses into a running tally.

quiz.question: What is the advantage of a synchronous counter over a ripple counter?
options: It uses fewer flip-flops
All bits update simultaneously, avoiding cumulative delay
It can count higher numbers

topics.title: Finite State Machines: Logic with Memory

hook.text: A vending machine needs to remember how many coins you've inserted. It has states.

buildup.text: A finite state machine has a set of states, transitions, and outputs — all defined by logic.

discovery.text: Flip-flops store the current state. Combinational logic computes the next state and output.

twist.text: Traffic lights, elevator controllers, and USB protocols are all finite state machines.

climax.text: CPUs are enormously complex state machines — each instruction triggers a sequence of states.

punchline.text: Remember the past, decide the future — a state machine is logic with memory.

quiz.question: What stores the current state in a finite state machine?
options: Capacitors that hold charge
Flip-flops that retain their values between clock cycles
Resistors that maintain a voltage level

topics.title: Clock Signals: The Heartbeat of Digital Circuits

hook.text: A clock signal toggles between 0 and 1 at a fixed rate. It's the heartbeat of every chip.

buildup.text: At each clock edge, flip-flops capture data, counters increment, and state machines advance.

discovery.text: Clock speed is measured in hertz. A 4 GHz processor ticks four billion times per second.

twist.text: Higher clock speed generates more heat. Modern chips throttle speed to manage thermal limits.

climax.text: Clock distribution networks span entire chips — ensuring every flip-flop ticks in sync.

punchline.text: No clock, no sync, no computing — the clock is the pulse that keeps order.

quiz.question: Why do faster clock speeds generate more heat?
options: More clock edges per second means more transistor switching, which dissipates energy as heat
The clock signal itself carries more voltage at higher frequencies
Faster clocks create electromagnetic radiation that heats nearby components

hook.text: In 1945 von Neumann proposed a computer that stores programs and data in the same memory.

buildup.text: The design has a CPU, memory, and I/O connected by buses. Fetch, decode, execute, repeat.

discovery.text: Storing programs in memory means the computer can modify its own instructions on the fly.

twist.text: The bottleneck: CPU and memory share one bus. Data and instructions compete for bandwidth.

climax.text: Almost every general-purpose computer today still follows von Neumann's basic plan.

punchline.text: One memory, one bus, one idea — von Neumann shaped modern computing.

quiz.question: What is the von Neumann bottleneck?
options: The CPU can't process more than one instruction at a time
Data and instructions share one memory bus, limiting throughput
Memory is too slow to keep up with the CPU's clock speed

hook.text: Every instruction goes through three stages: fetch from memory, decode, then execute.

buildup.text: The program counter holds the address. The CPU fetches the instruction at that address.

discovery.text: The decoder breaks the instruction into an opcode and operands. Then the ALU does the work.

twist.text: Pipelining overlaps stages — one instruction executes while the next is decoded and the next is fetched.

climax.text: Modern CPUs pipeline 15-20 stages deep, executing multiple instructions per clock cycle.

punchline.text: Fetch, decode, execute — three simple steps, billions of times per second.

quiz.question: How does pipelining improve CPU performance?
options: It makes each instruction execute faster
It overlaps different stages of multiple instructions, increasing throughput
It reduces the number of instructions needed for a task

topics.title: Cache Memory: Speed Close to the Core

hook.text: Main memory is fast, but the CPU is faster. Cache bridges the gap with tiny, ultra-fast storage.

buildup.text: L1 cache sits inside the core — small (64 KB) but accessible in 1-2 cycles.

discovery.text: L2 and L3 caches are larger but slower. The hierarchy trades size for speed.

twist.text: A cache miss forces the CPU to wait for main memory — tens of cycles lost.

climax.text: Programs that access data in order hit the cache often. Random access causes more misses.

punchline.text: Keep the most-used data close — cache hides memory's slowness from the CPU.

quiz.question: Why is L1 cache faster but smaller than L3 cache?
options: L1 uses a different type of transistor technology
Smaller memory can be placed closer to the core and accessed in fewer cycles
L1 cache operates at a higher voltage

topics.title: RISC vs CISC: Two Design Philosophies

hook.text: Should a processor have many complex instructions or fewer simple ones? Two camps disagree.

buildup.text: CISC packs lots of work into each instruction — x86 has thousands of instruction types.

discovery.text: RISC keeps instructions uniform and simple — each finishes in one cycle. ARM is RISC.

twist.text: Modern x86 chips decode complex instructions into micro-ops — CISC outside, RISC inside.

climax.text: ARM's RISC efficiency won mobile. x86's CISC backward compatibility dominates desktops.

punchline.text: Simple or complex — both paths converged toward the same speed.

quiz.question: How do modern x86 processors handle their complex instruction set?
options: They execute each complex instruction directly in hardware
They decode complex instructions into simpler micro-ops internally
They ignore complex instructions and only run simple ones

hook.text: Clock speeds plateaued around 2005. The solution: add more cores instead of going faster.

buildup.text: Each core runs its own instruction stream. Four cores can run four programs at once.

discovery.text: Hyper-threading lets one core handle two threads — keeping execution units busy.

twist.text: Not all software can use many cores. Amdahl's law limits the speedup from parallelism.

climax.text: Server chips now have 128 cores. GPUs have thousands of tiny cores for parallel workloads.

punchline.text: Can't go faster alone? Work together — parallelism is the future of speed.

quiz.question: What does Amdahl's law state about parallel computing?
options: Adding more cores always doubles performance
The serial portion of a program limits the maximum speedup from adding more cores
Parallel programs are always faster than serial ones

topics.title: System on Chip: Everything in One Package

hook.text: Your phone's main chip contains CPU, GPU, modem, AI accelerator, and more — all on one die.

buildup.text: System on Chip (SoC) integrates components that used to be separate chips on a motherboard.

discovery.text: On-chip communication is faster and uses less power than chip-to-chip wiring.

twist.text: SoC design requires expertise in digital, analog, RF, and power — all in one team.

climax.text: Apple's M-series, Qualcomm's Snapdragon, and Samsung's Exynos are all SoCs.

punchline.text: One chip to run the phone — SoC put an entire computer on a fingernail.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of a System on Chip design?
options: It eliminates the need for software altogether
On-chip integration reduces size, power, and latency compared to separate chips
SoCs are easier to manufacture than individual chips
